(B) Effect of Substituent on the Reactivity of the Benzene Ring

The substituent attached to the benzene ring also affects the reactivity of benzene ring in comparison with the unsubstituted benzene, this is called reactivity effect. Reactivity effect may be ring activating or deactivating.

i. Ring activating effect

The ortho/para directing groups release electrons to the ring by resonance making it electron rich. Thus, the attack of a second electrophile would be faster as compared to the benzene ring itself. Thus, the ortho/para directing species increase the reactivity of the benzene ring. They are ring activators and are referred to as activating groups. Halogens are the exceptions to this. It has been observed that halogens, though are ortho/para directing, are ring deactivators.

For example, the nitration of benzene (Section 16.8.5.2.2) requires concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid at 60°C, while nitration of phenol can easily occur with dilute nitric acid at 25°C as discussed earlier in this section. This is due to activating effect of –OH group.

ii. Ring deactivating effect

All meta directing groups and halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) withdraw electrons from the ring making it electron deficient. Thus in the presence of meta directing species, the attack of a second electrophile would be slower as compared to the benzene ring. Hence, these groups are ring deactivators.

For example, the nitration of benzene (Section 16.8.5.2.2) requires concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid at 60°C, while nitration of nitrobenzene can be even slower with concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid at 100°C as discussed earlier in this section. This is due to deactivating effect of –NO₂ group.

16.8.5.2.8 Making Polysubstituted Benzenes

Polysubstituted benzenes are the derivatives of benzene in which two or more hydrogen atoms have been substituted by other atoms or group of atoms. We have to keep in mind the activating and directing effect of first substituents on the ring while planning the synthesis of a polysubstituted benzene derivative.

For example, the synthesis of bromonitrobenzene from benzene require the introduction of –NO₂ and –Br groups in two consecutive electrophilic substitution reactions i.e. nitration and bromination. Either of the two substituents can be introduced into the benzene ring first and then the other. If benzene is first brominated and then nitrated, we will get mainly a mixture of o- and p-bromonitrobenzene because bromo group is ortho/para orienting.

However, if we want to prepare m-bromonitrobenzene, we shall carry out the nitration first and then bromination, because the nitro group is meta orienting.

Similarly, if we plan to synthesize nitro derivatives of phenol, we must do it by nitration of phenol. Nitration of phenol can be carried out by using dilute or concentrated nitric acid. Nitration with dilute nitric acid gives mainly ortho and para mono-nitrophenols (Section 16.8.5.2.7), but if we are using concentrated nitric acid, reaction cannot be stopped at mono-nitration stage and we get 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.

Draw the possible resonance structures for chlorobenzene and benzaldehyde.

(B) Effect of Substituent on the Reactivity of the Benzene Ring

The substituent attached to the benzene ring also affects the reactivity of benzene ring in comparison with the unsubstituted benzene, this is called reactivity effect. Reactivity effect may be ring activating or deactivating.

i. Ring activating effect

The ortho/para directing groups release electrons to the ring by resonance making it electron rich. Thus, the attack of a second electrophile would be faster as compared to the benzene ring itself. Thus, the ortho/para directing species increase the reactivity of the benzene ring. They are ring activators and are referred to as activating groups. Halogens are the exceptions to this. It has been observed that halogens, though are ortho/para directing, are ring deactivators.

For example, the nitration of benzene (Section 16.8.5.2.2) requires concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid at 60°C, while nitration of phenol can easily occur with dilute nitric acid at 25°C as discussed earlier in this section. This is due to activating effect of –OH group.

ii. Ring deactivating effect

All meta directing groups and halogens (F, Cl, Br, I) withdraw electrons from the ring making it electron deficient. Thus in the presence of meta directing species, the attack of a second electrophile would be slower as compared to the benzene ring. Hence, these groups are ring deactivators.

For example, the nitration of benzene (Section 16.8.5.2.2) requires concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid at 60°C, while nitration of nitrobenzene can be even slower with concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid at 100°C as discussed earlier in this section. This is due to deactivating effect of –NO₂ group.

Table 16.5 Orientation and Reactivity Effect of Some Common Groups

16.8.5.2.8 Making Polysubstituted Benzenes

Polysubstituted benzenes are the derivatives of benzene in which two or more hydrogen atoms have been substituted by other atoms or group of atoms. We have to keep in mind the activating and directing effect of first substituents on the ring while planning the synthesis of a polysubstituted benzene derivative.

For example, the synthesis of bromonitrobenzene from benzene require the introduction of –NO₂ and –Br groups in two consecutive electrophilic substitution reactions i.e. nitration and bromination. Either of the two substituents can be introduced into the benzene ring first and then the other. If benzene is first brominated and then nitrated, we will get mainly a mixture of o- and p-bromonitrobenzene because bromo group is ortho/para orienting.

However, if we want to prepare m-bromonitrobenzene, we shall carry out the nitration first and then bromination, because the nitro group is meta orienting.

Similarly, if we plan to synthesize nitro derivatives of phenol, we must do it by nitration of phenol. Nitration of phenol can be carried out by using dilute or concentrated nitric acid. Nitration with dilute nitric acid gives mainly ortho and para mono-nitrophenols (Section 16.8.5.2.7), but if we are using concentrated nitric acid, reaction cannot be stopped at mono-nitration stage and we get 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.
